messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] time-of-detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tracy,

If I'm not mistaken, time-of-detection models are normally used for estimating abundance, not occupancy. You can fit the abundance models in unmarked using the multinomPois() or gmultmix() functions. Each has a help page, and there is this vignette: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/cap-recap.pdf

Richard

Hello all,
I have single-visit point count data with spatial replicates, and so the replicates lack independence. Tracy

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] simultaneous bird counts in three areas as dependent variables
messages.body_plain:
Many Thanks
Andy.

I reviewed
the documents you suggested and have watched much of the webinar which I found
quite helpful. However, I have a fundamental question that I need to find the
answer to in order to figure out whether a hierarchical model is appropriate
for our data.

Here's the
key question at the moment: Is it possible to estimate detection probability
when there is no replication of bird counts per sample period? I think the answer
is no, but I may be missing something.

Our data set
involves monthly bird counts over several years.  Each month, there is a count in each of three
different geographic zones.

For example:

# birds

                june       july         aug         etc.

zone1    0              5              2

zone2    1              3              2

zone3    3              1              1

The birds
are capable of moving between zones, so the bird counts each month are not replicates
of an estimation of abundance in the zone. The number of birds in zone1 in june
is the only estimate of abundance in that zone for that month.

I also have
estimates of fruiting in each zone as covariates.

For this
data structure, is there an unmarked function such as pcount() or pcountOpen()
that will help with the issue of imperfect observation?

Or, as I
suspect, am I restricted to using a poisson regression with glm since I do not
have multiple visits per count?

Thanks,

Rhine

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rhine,

For pcountOpen(), "obsCovs" are only used for modeling detection probability when you collected data using the so-called "robust design" (which is always the preferred option). The possible covariate options for the 4 parameters are this:

lambda: siteCovs only
omega/gamma: siteCovs or yearlySiteCovs
p: siteCovs, yearlySiteCovs, or obsCovs (if you have the robust design)

Richard

messages.body_plain:
hi Ezequiel,
 SPACECAP fits individual encounter history models and unless you have a lot of recaptures you probably can't expect much with n = 6 observations.

 unmarked can fit multi-year models using either the pcount() function, where you could model year as a polynomial trend or in relation to fixed covariates, or you can use pcountOpen which fits a fully dynamic model.
An example of the former is here:
@article{kery2009trend,
  title={Trend estimation in populations with imperfect detection},
  author={Kery, M. and Dorazio, R.M. and Soldaat, L. and Van Strien, A. and Zuiderwijk, A. and Royle, J.A.},
  journal={Journal of Applied Ecology},
  volume={46},
  number={6},
  pages={1163--1172},
  year={2009},
  publisher={Wiley Online Library}
}

andy

messages.subject_clean: Modeling prey behavioral responses
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I set up camera traps at 22 locations over the course of a winter and would like to assess whether prey (deer) temporarily avoid sites when predators (wolves) are in the vicinity or have been recently.  I can see two strategies to do this, and would love any feedback on whether one makes more sense than the other (or some third option that I haven't thought of).

Strategy 1:
Divide the winter into 50 primary sampling occasions, each with 3 secondary occasions (days), then use "number of wolves detected" (or else predicted wolf abundance) in each primary occasion at each site as a yearly sampling covariate in pcountOpen models for deer.  If I understand these models correctly, "wolf abundance" could affect either deer gamma or omega (or both) but not deer lambda (since it's time-invariant).

Strategy 2:
Run a simple occu model where deer psi is constant (deer were detected at all sites at least once) but where "wolf presence" on a given day is used as a sampling covariate in the deer p function.  Then the interpretation would be along the lines of, "we know that deer occur in all sites, but when wolves are detected at a given site, deer are more/less/equally likely to be detected there".  Then I could also test for effects of time-lags in behavioral response as well.

In other words, both strategies would get at temporal rather than spatial predation avoidance.  I could see either of these working, but clearly if one was more robust, defensible, or appropriate than the other, I'd go with that.  Any feedback is very appreciated!
